title: Mixtures of geodesic factor analyzers on Riemannian homogeneous spaces
one_liner: Group curvy data into clusters where each group has its own shape of spread, not just one universal rounded blob.
lead: Real data lives on curved spaces, not flat grids: shapes traced on surfaces, positions on spheres, or paths twisted through space where the shortest route curves around obstacles. Older methods assumed all clusters spread out the same way — a round, symmetric cloud. This paper adds a new lens: each cluster can have its own stretched or squashed shape.

problem.h2: Why round clouds fail on curved ground
paras: Imagine sorting people by body shape. A naive approach: measure them on a flat 2D plane (height and shoulder width) and assume each group — tall sprinters, stocky wrestlers — spreads out in a round blob. That works on a plane.

But real body shapes live on a sphere, because you can rotate a person in 3D space. Rotate a cluster, and it looks the same — but measure it on the flat plane after spinning, and the blob changes shape. Worse: a tall-and-narrow cluster (one group is all long limbs) stays long and narrow even if you spin it. Round-blob math misses that.

callout.html: Existing methods assume all clusters spread out identically and symmetrically, failing to capture groups that are stretched in specific directions on curved spaces.

steps.text: Points on a curved space: faces on the shape-of-skulls sphere, or brain structures twisted in hyperbolic 3D.
Use a curved ruler (geodesic distance) that follows the surface, not straight-line shortcuts across empty space.
Each group gets a direction of stretch — one cluster might be thin along one axis, fat along another.
Assign each point to the cluster whose stretched shape fits it best, accounting for curve and stretch.
Re-fit the shapes, re-assign points until the clustering stops changing.

paras: Instead of one universal round-blob formula for how each cluster spreads, this method lets each cluster have a directional shape: an ellipse (or ellipsoid in 3D), stretched differently along different curves through the curved space. The shape lives and breathes on the curved surface itself.

hidden.h2: The directional stretch of each cluster
hidden.name: anisotropy per cluster
paras: Anisotropy means uneven stretch — some directions compressed, others spread wide. Each cluster has its own anisotropy: the pattern of which directions are squeezed and which are loose.

The paper estimates anisotropy by measuring how far points in each cluster deviate along different directions on the curve, using a method called a geodesic factor model: it breaks the overall scatter into a core spread (the centroid's neighborhood) plus directional stretch patterns.

heat.caption: Darker means more scatter along that direction. Each cluster's darkest cells show where it stretches widest.

reads.html: Each cluster is not a round blob — it is fat in some directions and thin in others, and the paper measures that shape.
A geodesic factor model decomposes the spread pattern on the curved surface into principal directions of variance per mixture component.

mechanism.h2: Why stretched shapes fix the problem
paras: On a curved surface, a truly round cluster is rare. Real clusters align with natural patterns. One group of brain shapes might be uniformly tall (big variation along one anatomical direction, small along others). The old method forced roundness, inflating the small-variation directions to compensate, and mislabeled points near the cluster edge.

By letting each cluster be stretched differently, the method matches the actual data shape. A tall-and-thin cluster is modeled as tall-and-thin. A round cluster is modeled as round. When a model matches reality, points in the true cluster score much higher under their correct cluster than under false ones, because the real shape is tight and consistent. The old round-blob model wastes information on dimensions that are not actually spread, so many points near cluster boundaries tie or flip to the wrong cluster. More data helps because each new point sampled from a cluster lands in predictable places along that cluster's true stretch directions. With 10 points, noise can hide the stretch. With 1000 points, the stretch pattern is undeniable and the algorithm finds it reliably.

stages.s: Compute geodesic distances from each point to each cluster center
Score how well this point fits this cluster's shape

math.words: For each cluster, score a point by how far it sits from the cluster center along each direction, weighted by the stretch in that direction. Add these up and subtract from a constant to get a likelihood.
math.equation: log p(x|k) = const - 0.5 * sum_j (residual_j^2 / stretch_j) - 0.5 * log(det(Sigma_k))
symbols: probability that point x belongs to cluster k
how far the point sits from center along direction j, measured on the curve
how much variance is allowed along direction j (the j-th eigenvalue)
the covariance matrix for cluster k, living on the manifold
a volume term that scales with cluster size

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Cluster A: center at (north pole), stretch [8, 2, 1].
Point x nearby at distance 1.0 from center.
Correct stretch gives higher score: -0.1 > -0.19, so point stays in A.

math.note: The smaller the residuals and the larger the allowed stretch, the higher the score — a good fit. Clusters with natural anisotropy (one direction fat, others thin) fit real data without forcing roundness.

bars.h2: How much better does it sort?

charts.title: Old method (round blobs)
charts.note: Round blobs waste information; misses natural cluster stretches.

charts.title: This paper (geodesic factor model)
charts.note: Each cluster's true shape is modeled, so boundaries are clearer and points sort correctly.

items.b: Data doesn't actually live on the claimed curve.
items.html: If your data is really Euclidean (like pixel values in an image) but you measure it on a sphere, the method will overfit and learn spurious stretches.

items.b: Not enough data to estimate cluster stretches.
items.html: With few points per cluster, the anisotropy estimates are noisy. You may overfit individual noise bumps as real cluster structure.
If the manifold is wrong (e.g., you think it is a sphere but it is a torus), cluster shapes will be distorted, and boundaries will not line up correctly.
When data truly does live on a known curved space and the number of clusters and dimensionality are reasonable, the method recovers the true cluster structure.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Generate 200 synthetic points on a sphere, forming 3 clusters. Cluster 1 is tight (uniform spread in all directions). Cluster 2 is stretched along the north-south axis (fat north-to-south, thin east-west). Cluster 3 is randomly scattered. Run the old round-blob method and the new geodesic factor method. Plot the final cluster assignments as colors on the sphere surface and measure accuracy.
demo.closing: The new method should sort all 200 correctly (or near it); the old method should mislabel 30–40 points, especially along cluster boundaries where shapes overlap.
